questions.question_text: In a child with reactive attachment disorder (RAD), which of the following areas is least likely to improve with treatment?
questions.explanation: Despite the pervasiveness and severity of RAD, there have been very few studies of outcomes with or without treatment. In accord with initial observations of early emotional deprivation, the symptoms and prognosis appear to depend on the age when the deprivation begins, its severity, the child’s temperament, and the duration of the deprivation situation. Earlier interventions appear to have a greater likelihood of improving outcomes than later interventions. Cognitive and language development, motor development, and self-care are more likely to improve than problems with social development (O’Connor and Rutter 2000; Rutter and O’Connor 2004; Zeanah 2000).

questions.question_text: In the Pavlovian conditioning model of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), an increased heart rate represents which of the following?
questions.explanation: One of the earliest and best replicated PTSD findings is heightened autonomic (heart rate, skin conductance) and facial electromyographic reactivity to external trauma-related stimuli, such as combat sounds and film clips, as well as to internal mental imagery of the traumatic event. These findings have been interpreted within a framework of Pavlovian conditioning, in which the traumatic event serves as the unconditioned stimulus, the emotional response to it serves as the unconditioned response, trauma-related cues serve as conditioned stimuli, and the physiological reactions serve as conditioned responses.

questions.question_text: What is the most replicated functional neuroimaging abnormality in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?

options.text: Decreased prefrontal cortex blood flow and metabolism.
Volume abnormalities in both gray and white matter.

questions.explanation: The most replicated functional neuroimaging abnormality in PTSD has been hyporesponsivity of ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC). A current neurocircuitry model of PTSD posits that vmPFC fails to inhibit amygdala. Diminished vmPFC activity may also underlie the reduced retention of extinction of conditioned fear found in PTSD, which may confer difficulty in recovering from the effects of trauma (Hughes and Shin 2011; Pitman et al. 2012). Decreased prefrontal cortex blood flow and metabolism is seen in depression, lateral and third ventricular enlargement is seen in schizophrenia, and volume abnormalities in gray and white matter are seen in autism spectrum disorders.

questions.question_text: What is the earliest developmental age at which reactive attachment disorder (RAD) may be diagnosed?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 describes the essential feature of RAD as absent or grossly underdeveloped attachment between the child and putative caregiving adults. Children with RAD are believed to have the capacity to form selective attachments, but because of their early development, they fail to show selective attachments. This diagnosis should not be made in children who are developmentally unable to form selective attachments; therefore, the child must be cognitively at least 9 months old.

questions.question_text: Which of the following populations has its own subtype of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in DSM-5?
questions.explanation: Because the evidence does not support use of adult criteria for PTSD in preschool children, criteria for a new diagnostic subtype (PTSD for children 6 years and younger) have been added in DSM-5. This is an advance from the special developmental considerations in DSM-IV-TR (American Psychiatric Association 2000) for specific diagnosis of PTSD in preschool children. Research with traumatized preschool children indicates that they require fewer criteria based on functional impairment from PTSD symptoms and that they have somewhat different responses to stress. The criteria for PTSD in children younger than age 6 highlight symptom differences, such as demonstrating trauma reenactment through play and experiencing frightening dreams not clearly related to the traumatic event (Scheeringa et al. 2011).

questions.question_text: What is the only class of medication shown to be effective in reducing the full range of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms?
questions.explanation: SSRIs are the only medications shown to be effective in reducing the full range of PTSD symptoms (Brady et al. 2000; Davidson et al. 1996; van der Kolk et al. 1994).

questions.question_text: Which widely used medication class may interfere with extinction learning and increase the risk of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after a traumatic event?
questions.explanation: Although many clinicians employ benzodiazepines for acute stress disorder and PTSD, with increased use from 2003 to 2010 (Hawkins 2012), some, including the Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense (2010), caution against using them for PTSD due to theoretical risks of interference with extinction learning, based on animal and very limited human research. Benzodiazepines might increase PTSD development with early use or interfere with extinction-based psychotherapies.

questions.question_text: According to the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP), what initial treatment is recommended for children with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?

options.text: Pharmacotherapy with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI).

questions.explanation: For the treatment of children and adolescents with PTSD, the AACAP advises beginning with trauma-focused CBT and adding an SSRI if severity of symptoms indicates a need for more interventions (Cohen et al. 2007). The AACAP Practice Parameter (Cohen et al. 2010) endorses consideration of SSRIs but cautions that due to possible hyperarousal, with irritability, poor sleep, or inattention, SSRIs may not be an optimal treatment when used alone in the absence of psychotherapy. A large double-blind study of sertraline compared with placebo found no benefit of sertraline in children (Robb et al. 2010), and a small double-blind study of sertraline to prevent PTSD in burned children indicated a marginal benefit based on parent but not child report (Stoddard et al. 2011). Despite wide clinical use, no evidence-based study has established the benefit of benzodiazepines, propranolol, or clonidine for PTSD in children, and no evidence-based study supports antipsychotics for child PTSD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following means of exposure to a traumatic event does not meet criterion A for acute stress disorder or posttraumatic stress disorder?

options.text: Witnessing in person an event that occurred to others.
Learning that the event occurred to a close relative or close friend.
Collecting the remains of the deceased.
Repeatedly hearing the details of the event.

questions.explanation: Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the event does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies, or pictures, unless this exposure is work-related.

questions.question_text: To qualify for a DSM-5 diagnosis of adjustment disorder, symptoms must occur within what period following onset of a stressor and must resolve within what period following removal of the stressor?

options.text: Symptom occurrence within 2 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 6 months of stressor's removal.
Symptom occurrence within 3 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 12 months of stressor's removal.
Symptom occurrence within 4 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 9 months of stressor's removal.
Symptom occurrence within 6 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 12 months of stressor's removal.
Symptom occurrence within 3 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 6 months of stressor's removal.

correct_answer.text: Symptom occurrence within 3 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 6 months of stressor's removal.

correct_answers.text: Symptom occurrence within 3 months of stressor's onset and symptom resolution within 6 months of stressor's removal.

questions.explanation: According to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, an adjustment disorder requires the development of clinically significant emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor. The symptoms must occur within 3 months of the onset of the stressor (Criterion A) and must resolve within 6 months after the stressor is removed (Criterion E).

questions.question_text: What is the most prominent focus of prolonged exposure therapy for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?

options.text: Targeted homework assignments designed to reshape dysfunctional cognitive beliefs that interfere with recovery.
Mindfulness exercises to enhance coping strategies.
Conjoint sessions to reduce the impact of the patient's PTSD symptoms on his or her intimate partner.
Repeated imaginal and in vivo exposures to enhance extinction of traumatic memories and decrease cue reactivity.
Intensive debriefing to prevent consolidation of traumatic memories.

correct_answer.text: Repeated imaginal and in vivo exposures to enhance extinction of traumatic memories and decrease cue reactivity.

correct_answers.text: Repeated imaginal and in vivo exposures to enhance extinction of traumatic memories and decrease cue reactivity.

questions.explanation: At present, the most strongly supported and evidence-based psychotherapies are structured trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral approaches such as prolonged exposure therapy (PE; Foa et al. 2005), which has shown excellent treatment results across a range of populations with PTSD, including PTSD following sexual assault or combat trauma. PE focuses most prominently on 1) repeated imaginal exposure to the primary trauma memories to enhance extinction generally over the course of weekly 90-minute sessions and 2) in vivo exposures to decrease cue reactivity and avoidance. Trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) approaches generally target emotion processing of the trauma to enhance extinction, focusing on decreasing avoidance behaviors and reducing negative emotional reactivity. CBT approaches may also include cognitive work focused on distorted beliefs about the self and safety that may arise as a result of the trauma (e.g., see Schmertz et al. 2014). These treatments build on the notion that PTSD is a condition of impeded recovery from an acute reaction to trauma and that much of the psychopathology centers on failure of extinction of fear responses and development of maladaptive cognitions and avoidance behaviors that interfere with recovery. Psychoeducation about PTSD is an important initial component of all CBT approaches, and some approaches also teach stress management techniques such as breathing and relaxation skills (Schmertz et al. 2014).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements does not describe a way in which the presentation of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in preschool children differs from that in older children, adolescents, and adults?

options.text: In young children, spontaneous and intrusive memories may manifest as play reenactment.
In young children, intrusive memories may not necessarily appear to be distressing.
In young children, it may not be possible to ascertain that frightening dream content is related to the traumatic event.
In young children, responses to stress are similar to those seen in adults.
In young children, dissociative reactions involving reexperiencing of the traumatic event may be expressed in play.

correct_answer.text: In young children, responses to stress are similar to those seen in adults.

correct_answers.text: In young children, responses to stress are similar to those seen in adults.

questions.explanation: Because the evidence does not support use of adult criteria for PTSD in preschool children, criteria for a new diagnostic subtype (PTSD for children 6 years and younger) have been added in DSM-5. Research with traumatized preschool children indicates that they require fewer criteria based on functional impairment from PTSD symptoms and that they have somewhat different responses to stress. The criteria for PTSD in children younger than age 6 years highlight symptom differences in this age group, such as demonstrating trauma reenactment through play and experiencing frightening dreams not clearly related to the traumatic event (Scheeringa et al. 2011).

questions.question_text: What is the essential feature of reactive attachment disorder (RAD)?

options.text: Absent attachment between child and putative caregiving adults.
Developmental delays in language and cognition.

correct_answer.text: Absent attachment between child and putative caregiving adults.

correct_answers.text: Absent attachment between child and putative caregiving adults.

questions.explanation: DSM-5 identifies the essential feature of RAD as absent or grossly underdeveloped attachment between a child and putative caregiving adults. The history usually includes prolonged separation, severe neglect and/or abuse, or living in institutional settings from an early age. Children with RAD can have compromised emotional regulation; however, it is not an essential feature. Although stereotypies, developmental delays in language and cognition, and evidence of malnutrition are possible in RAD, they are associated features and are not essential to the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old child exhibits overly familiar behavior, often crossing boundaries, with no reticence to approach strangers and minimal hesitation in going off with unfamiliar adults. There is a history of consistent parenting since birth. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
questions.explanation: There are some differences in manifestations of disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED) from early childhood through adolescence. Young children with DSED fail to show reticence to approach, engage with, and even go off with unfamiliar adults. In preschool children, verbal and social intrusiveness appears prominent and is often accompanied by attention-seeking behavior (Tizard and Rees 1975; Zeanah et al. 2002, 2005). Verbal and physical overfamiliarity continue through middle childhood, accompanied by inauthentic expressions of emotion. In adolescence, indiscriminate behavior extends to peers, with more “superficial” peer relationships and conflicts. Adult manifestations of the disorder are unknown.

questions.question_text: To qualify for a DSM-5 diagnosis of acute stress disorder, symptoms must persist for what duration after a traumatic event?
questions.explanation: The DSM-5 criteria for acute stress disorder require the presence of at least 9 of 14 symptoms in any of five categories—intrusion symptoms, negative mood, dissociative symptoms, avoidance symptoms, and arousal symptoms—beginning or worsening after the traumatic event and persisting for 3 days to 1 month after the trauma.

questions.question_text: Which of the following early intervention strategies in trauma survivors can actually increase stress and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms?

options.text: Conducting a debriefing focused on the traumatic experience.
Facilitating communication with friends or family.
Organizing a community council for displaced survivors.

correct_answer.text: Conducting a debriefing focused on the traumatic experience.

correct_answers.text: Conducting a debriefing focused on the traumatic experience.

questions.explanation: Supportive care, including communication and contact with social supports, and medical assistance (Zohar et al. 2009) are recommended as first-line interventions for trauma survivors instead of requiring or encouraging individuals to relay or debrief their traumatic experiences. Psychological critical incident stress debriefing (CISD), although initially found useful, more recently was shown in group settings either to have no effect or to increase stress and PTSD symptoms, potentially by altering the course of or undermining naturally occurring coping mechanisms (Rose et al. 2002; van Emmerik et al. 2002).

questions.question_text: In studies examining biological responses to trauma-related stimuli in subjects with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which of the following findings has been repeatedly confirmed?
questions.explanation: Over the past three decades, the growth of the biological PTSD literature has been explosive (Pitman et al. 2012). Discoveries of biological abnormalities in PTSD have helped to counteract skepticism regarding a disorder that is largely based on self-report and to promote its now widespread acceptance. One of the earliest and best replicated PTSD findings is heightened autonomic (heart rate, skin conductance) and facial electromyographic reactivity to external, trauma-related stimuli, such as combat sounds and film clips, as well as to internal, mental imagery of the traumatic event. Subjects with PTSD have also been found to show heightened electromyographic responses and more consistently heightened autonomic responses to startling stimuli (Pole 2007). Elevated startle responses suggest sensitization of the nervous system.

questions.question_text: Which of the following changes in sleep architecture has been demonstrated in individuals with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
questions.explanation: Support for DSM-5 criterion E6, sleep disturbance, has not been straightforward, but more Stage 1 sleep and less slow-wave sleep, indicative of shallower sleeping, have been demonstrated in patients with PTSD (Kobayashi et al. 2007).

questions.question_text: Which of the following best characterizes the quality of peer relationships among adolescents with disinhibited social engagement disorder (DSED)?
questions.explanation: There are some differences in manifestations of DSED from early childhood through adolescence. Young children with DSED fail to show reticence to approach, engage with, and even go off with unfamiliar adults. In preschool children, verbal and social intrusiveness appears prominent and is often accompanied by attention-seeking behavior (Tizard and Rees 1975; Zeanah et al. 2002, 2005). Verbal and physical overfamiliarity continue through middle childhood, accompanied by inauthentic expressions of emotion. In adolescence, indiscriminate behavior extends to peers, with more “superficial” peer relationships and conflicts. Adult manifestations of the disorder are unknown.

questions.question_text: An 85-year-old woman who lost her husband to cancer more than a year ago is sent to you for consultation. Since her husband's death, she has experienced intense sorrow and longing for him. In addition, on most days she has difficulty accepting that he is dead, and she often blames herself for his death. She is angry with and untrusting of her family, feels alone, and desires "to be with him." What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder.

correct_answer.text: Other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder.

correct_answers.text: Other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder.

questions.explanation: The severe and persistent grief and mourning reactions that characterize this woman’s symptom presentation meet criteria for the proposed diagnosis persistent complex bereavement disorder, which appears in Section III (“Conditions for Further Study”) of DSM-5. However, because the proposed criteria sets in Section III are not intended for clinical use, the appropriate diagnosis in this case would be other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder (persistent complex bereavement disorder). This woman’s symptoms do not meet criteria for major depressive disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, or an adjustment disorder. The “other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder” category applies to presentations in which symptoms characteristic of a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning predominate but do not meet the full criteria for any of the disorders in the trauma- and stressor-related disorders diagnostic class.
